assets.title: Mary McCoy
assets.description: Mary McCoy recalls her family's forced move uphill when the creek was dammed - including the dramatic moment their dragged four-bedroom house nearly toppled when the chains snapped. Hear how they rebuilt a life on that hill, and why Mary still calls it her "beautiful house."
assets.about:
Mary McCoy was born in 1945 near Caney Creek, on land her grandmother
owned. With cattle, a big barn, and a thriving garden, the family lived
well, until the creek was dammed and the family was forced to move to a
smaller plot further up the hill. The family dragged their four-bedroom
home uphill on straps and chains – a nearby truck helped them avert
disaster when the chains snapped and the house fell backwards. On the
hill, living was harder: watering the garden meant carrying buckets by
hand, and the family waited a decade for electricity. Later, Mary spent
nearly 40 years in hospital work and always looked back fondly at the
‘beautiful house’ on the hill.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Michael Cooksey, respected
Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: DJ Vann
assets.description: Hear DJ talk about his early years, when his family relied on hunting, fishing, gardening, and rearing animals to sustain themselves through the hard times. His recording paints a rich picture of Cherokee life – self-sufficiency, community, and connection to the land.
assets.about:
DJ Vann’s childhood was steeped in the Cherokee language. Growing up near
Bunch and Greasy, Oklahoma, both of his parents spoke Cherokee at home –
starkly different from today’s Cherokee people, only one generation
later. Hear DJ talk about his early years, when his family relied on
hunting, fishing, gardening, and rearing animals to sustain themselves
through the hard times. While DJ worked alongside his father building
bridges and railroad ties, there was still time for baseball, using balls
sewn from old blue jeans. His recording paints a rich picture of Cherokee
life – self-sufficiency, community, and connection to the land.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language
speaker.

assets.title: Martin Ballou
assets.description: Raised near Ballou, Oklahoma, Martin Ballou walked three miles each way, whatever the weather, to get to school. Hear him remember those early, difficult school days, when he spoke only Cherokee.
assets.about:
Raised near Ballou, Oklahoma, Martin Ballou walked three miles each way,
whatever the weather, to get to school. Hear him remember those early,
difficult school days, when he spoke only Cherokee. It wasn’t until a new
teacher, also a speaker, helped him bridge the language divide that
things started to make sense. His childhood was steeped in Cherokee
tradition and community, centered around the church. Later, Martin’s
commitment to his faith saw him serve as a deacon and song leader for 40
years. He also spent 10 years in the U.S. Marine Corps. Martin’s memories
paint a rich picture of Cherokee life and community in twentieth-century
America – and all that has changed for both better and worse.

The interviewer is Guy Soldier, respected Cherokee first language
speaker.

assets.title: Toney Cornshucker
assets.description: Toney was born in 1940, “across the creek” in Cloud Creek. Listen in as he recalls a Cherokee childhood in mid-century America, working with and living off the land.
assets.about:
Toney was born in 1940, “across the creek” in Cloud Creek.
Listen in as he recalls a Cherokee childhood in mid-century America,
working with and living off the land. Toney was raised by his
grandmother, Jenny Birdchopper, who survived the Trail of Tears as a
young girl. She shared memories of the removal with Toney – the loss and
sadness, and the people buried along the way. Despite the devastating
upheaval, Jenny Birdchopper carried deep traditional Cherokee knowledge.
Toney recalls a community built on shared history, support and faith –
both Christian and traditional.

The interviewer is Guy Soldier, respected Cherokee first language
speaker.

assets.title: Charley & Mary McCoy
assets.description: Married for decades, Charley and Mary McCoy’s childhood memories are echoes of one another. Listen in to hear what it was like growing up in various communities of the Cherokee Nation, living close to the land, gathering and growing food, and living well even with little money.
assets.community: Dry Creek and Caney Creek/Barber, Oklahoma
assets.about:
Married for decades, Charley and Mary McCoy’s childhood memories are
echoes of one another. Listen in to hear what it was like growing up in
various communities of the Cherokee Nation, living close to the land,
gathering and growing food, and living well even with little money.
Their Cherokee-speaking communities were centered around church, shared
values, and self-sufficiency. Both also remember injustice – the
families of Charley and Mary were impoverished following the loss of
valuable land to the government authorities’ ‘improvement’ schemes. The
‘theft’, as they call it, still impacts their families and communities
today, although Mary and Charley’s hard work and dedication saw them
progress in their careers. While raising six children, Mary worked as an
emergency room nurse. Charley served in the Army and took jobs in
construction, with Cherokee Nation and for Northeastern College,
Tahlequah.

The interviewers are Guy Soldier and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee
first language speakers.

assets.title: Jerry & Mary Scott
assets.description: Husband and wife, Jerry and Mary Scott grew up speaking Cherokee. Hear them remembering childhoods in rural Cherokee communities, living in homes with no water or electricity.
assets.about:
Husband and wife, Jerry and Mary Scott grew up speaking Cherokee. Hear
them remembering childhoods in rural Cherokee communities, living in
homes with no water or electricity. Without toys, Jerry says they made
their own fun, spending long days in the woods, playing hide and seek,
kick the can, and during one memorable day, chasing down an owl. Mary
remembers hauling laundry down to a spring for washing, a community
activity, and traditional ways of gathering, growing, preserving, and
preparing foods. Alongside memories of hunting foxes late into the
night, and the childhood magic of believing in Santa Claus, are the
stark financial realities their families faced after the loss of
earners. This is deeply grounded insight into Cherokee family life.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language
speaker.

assets.title: Edward Bunch & Mack Flynn
assets.description: Friends and co-workers Mack Flynn and Eddie Bunch reflect on Cherokee childhoods in 1960s and '70s Oklahoma. Listen as Mack recalls learning fluent Cherokee overnight at age six from cousins his family took in, and Eddie remembers dirt-floor kitchens and tables always full for whoever arrived hungry in Greasy.
assets.about:
Friends and co-workers Mack Flynn and Eddie Bunch reflect on childhoods growing up Cherokee in 1960s and ’70s Oklahoma. Listen as Mack, a native-English speaker, remembers a house full of Cherokee-speaking cousins his family had taken in, and the aunt and uncle who spoke no English. That daily immersion meant that as a six-year-old he started speaking fluent Cherokee, seemingly overnight. Eddie recalls his childhood home in Greasy, and years spent catching chickens for a living. Kitchens had dirt floors that warmed as food cooked, and tables were always full for whoever arrived hungry – like one man who arrived worse for wear and mistook the scrap pan for soup.

The interviewers are Guy Soldier, Dianna Guffey and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: DJ & Francis McCarter
assets.description: Born in a house in Pumpkin Hollow, DJ McCarter’s early adulthood was spent playing guitar in dance halls before a profound spiritual experience drew him to 33 years of preaching. His wife Francis remembers walking up a hill at midnight to church, staying close to her father as he carried a coal-oil light through the dark.
assets.about:
Born in a house in Pumpkin Hollow, DJ McCarter’s early adulthood was
spent playing guitar in dance halls and hauling concrete. Hear as he
remembers the profound spiritual experience that drew him to the church
– what felt like a physical and audible command from God. DJ is still
preaching, 33 years later. His wife of more than 50 years, Francis,
remembers walking up a hill at midnight to get to church, staying close
to her father who carried a coal-oil light through the dark. The
recording combines these personal histories with extensive examples of
fluent conversational Cherokee, a rich source of linguistic, cultural
and historical knowledge.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language
speaker.

assets.title: Dora Dunn & Elsie Pritchett
assets.description: Elsie Pritchett and Dora Dunn are aunt and niece, four years apart, raised on the dirt roads of Dry Creek where every house held a relation. Listen as they trade memories: riding a horse-drawn wagon to the Barber store, cream kept cold in the spring water and an uncle’s payday holler: “We’re going to town!”
assets.about:
Elsie Pritchett and Dora Dunn are aunt and niece, four years apart,
raised on the dirt roads of Dry Creek where every house held a relation.
Listen as they trade memories: riding a horse-drawn wagon to the Barber
store, cream kept cold in the spring water and an uncle’s payday holler:
“We’re going to town!” At school, Cherokee children sat through lessons
in English, then handed in blank test papers until the school cook
stepped in to translate. Dora credits prayer with scoring 95% in a
syllabary test, a text she couldn’t read. Even after six years in
Germany, she never lost a word of Cherokee.

The interviewers are Michael Cooksey and Mitch Holcomb, respected
Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Bird Wolfe
assets.description: Listen to Bird Wolfe as he remembers growing up in Oklahoma’s Rocky Mountain, stories of Cherokee land, labor and belief remembered from the inside.
assets.about:
Bird Wolfe grew up in a home where everyone spoke Cherokee. Listen to
Bird as he remembers growing up in Oklahoma’s Rocky Mountain. After
quitting school in the seventh grade, he helped his father provide for
the family, picking strawberries and beans, clearing rocks and plowing
gardens with mules. Back then, a dollar felt like riches, but the real
living came out of the woods – deer, rabbits and squirrel, blackberries
and wild plums and grapes hanging along the roadside. Listen to the
stories of Cherokee land, labor and belief remembered from the inside.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Michael Cooksey, respected
Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Naomi "ᏣᏁᏂ" Stone
assets.description: Naomi Stone grew up at Greasy, Oklahoma. Hear her think back on barefoot summers in the woods, sticky with wild blueberries and blackberries, and hiding when it was time to plant corn, so she didn’t have to help. Bathing and laundry meant plunging into the icy spring across the road.
assets.about:
Naomi Stone grew up at Greasy, Oklahoma. The family home was small and
crowded, so Naomi and her siblings spent days outside. Hear her think
back on barefoot summers in the woods, sticky with wild blueberries and
blackberries, and hiding when it was time to plant corn, so she didn’t
have to help. Bathing and laundry meant plunging into the icy spring
across the road. Born into a Cherokee-speaking home and community, Naomi
was forced to speak English at school and physically punished for
speaking Cherokee. Now, as a community elder, she misses hearing the
language, so took a job working with – and talking to – preschoolers in
Cherokee.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee
first language speakers.

assets.title: Felix & Leroy Sanders
assets.description: Leroy Sanders and his Uncle Felix share boyhood stories of killing squirrels with rocks, and of Leroy running away at eleven on a train with a hobo. As an adult, Leroy and his wife took in 58 foster children.
assets.about:
Leroy Sanders has led an eventful life. Listen to him and his Uncle Felix talk about their early lives, from killing squirrels with rocks – because Leroy’s father wouldn’t let them use a gun – to Leroy running away from home. He talks about leaving his family in Chicago at just eleven, riding a train with a hobo for two days, and getting off at Stilwell, Oklahoma, where his grandfather lived. His parents came and took him home – and a month later he did the same thing again. After a tumultuous childhood, Leroy spent his adult life creating a stable home for other children. He and his wife took in an incredible 58 foster children over the years, giving them a safe, happy place to live when they needed it.

The interviewers are Guy Soldier and Dianna Guffey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Randy Duncan
assets.description: Born bald and nicknamed "Uncle Roy" after a hairless old man in town, Randy Duncan remembers growing up as a twin. As an adult he spent twenty-five years repairing the power lines he once saw sparking as a teenager.
assets.about:
Randy Duncan was bald when he was born, so family called him ‘Uncle Roy’ after a hairless old man in their town. Listen as he talks about being a twin in a Cherokee family, his mother driving him and his siblings to Dahlonegah every day to catch the school bus, and the traditional foods and medicines of his childhood. As a teen, Randy remembers boys in his hometown felling a tree onto a power line, leaving it sparking. As an adult, he repaired those same lines – working for Okark Electric for twenty-five years. He calls it one of the most dangerous jobs in the world. Randy is now an elder in his community. His story shows the connection between traditional wisdom, community bonds, and the natural world.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language speaker

assets.title: Janet Navarro
assets.description: Janet Navarro traces two childhoods — carefree days with her grandparents at Cherry Tree filled with crawdads and redbud-root toothbrushes, and the one the state took from her when it placed her in boarding school, a loss she later fought not to repeat with her own grandchildren.
assets.about:
Janet Navarro was four when her father died, and nine or ten when the state put her and her siblings into boarding schools. Before that there was Cherry Tree and her grandparents. Listen as Janet recounts those early memories: Granny hanging clean sheets to dry on trees, biscuits with mustard, wild onions and crawdads from the creek with redbud root for a toothbrush. Decades later, when authorities moved to take Janet’s grandchildren, she fought to keep them with family. Janet’s is a story of two childhoods – the carefree days her grandparents gave her at Cherry Tree, and the one the state took her into.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.title: Michael Pritchett
assets.description: Michael Pritchett's grandmother never let anyone leave hungry, and he shares how her kitchen taught him to cook and mend in a childhood of open doors, summer creek days, and playing catcher for his father's coaching.
assets.about:
Nobody left Michael Pritchett's grandmother's house hungry. She fed everyone who walked through the door. She also taught Michael to cook, to mend, and to work – skills he’d need for a self-sufficient adulthood. Listen in as he remembers summers in Sallisaw Creek, playing catcher with his father as coach, and a childhood where nobody locked a door. Ask him the best time of his life and he doesn't hesitate: school at Greasy. Michael's story traces how much of a man's life can be shaped in one grandmother's kitchen, and how far that open door still reaches.

The interviewers are Michael Cooksey and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Bud Foreman
assets.description: Lost while hunting possum as a boy, Bud Foreman found his way home by firefly light, and he shares that same resourcefulness in memories of helping build the church his family still worships in near Cloud.
assets.about:
Out possum hunting alone as a boy, Bud Foreman's coal oil lamp ran dry. In the dark, he gathered lightning bugs, stuck them to his clothes, and followed their glow home, thanking God all the way. Born in the hollows near Cloud, he helped build the little church on the hill, which still stands to this day. Gospel music anchored his family's life, from four-day singing gatherings at Cedar Tree to selling records at local carnivals. Hear him remember his grandparents and their perseverance and faith through hardship. His memories preserve the spirit, ingenuity, and deep communal faith of early Cherokee hollow life.

The interviewer is Guy Soldier, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.description: Harry Daugherty shares memories of a rootless childhood on "the hill" at Oak Ridge, playing country music in bars during his chaotic early adulthood, before a voice on the road twenty-eight years ago told him to go home and go to church.
assets.about:
Harry Daugherty grew up on "the hill" at Oak Ridge, where the teachers got down on their knees to shoot marbles with the boys and climbed trees. He lost his mother young, was passed to an aunt, then taken to California by an uncle who taught him how to drive by tossing the keys before leaving. Hear him remember playing country and western in bars, the chaos of his early adulthood, and then the voice he heard on a road twenty-eight years ago telling him to go home and go to church.

assets.description: Taken to California at twelve after his mother's death and back home at eighteen, Harry Daugherty reflects on fifteen years laying telephone line, hopping boxcars to Texas, and his nephews' encounter with the little people riding lizards.
assets.about:
At twelve, after his mother died at Talihina, Harry Daugherty was taken to California by an uncle who "always wanted a boy." He came home at eighteen on a three-day bus. Listen as he reflects on fifteen years laying telephone line across the country; on hopping boxcars to travel to Texas and the mystical little people his twin nephews once saw riding lizards. Harry’s rich memories paint a picture of tightknit Cherokee community in northeastern Oklahoma.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.title: Lillie Vann
assets.description: Letting cows into the corn patch as a child and growing up on squirrel, poke salad and possum grapes, Lillie Vann shares traditional remedies like red oak bark for colds — a life shaped by knowing what the land provides.
assets.about:
Lillie Vann and her sister let the cows into the corn patch while their parents were off in the strawberry fields, then threw hoes around to scratch out the footprints. They were found out anyway. Born in 1939, one of eight children sleeping scattered across the floor, she grew up on what the land gave: squirrel, frog legs, turtle, quail, poke salad, persimmons, possum grapes. She still eats acorns straight off the tree. Hear as she shares healing wisdom her elders used in place of western medicine: red oak bark for colds, honey locust bark for failing eyes. Lillie tells her life through a lens of abundance – what the land can provide if only you know where to look.

The interviewers are Guy Soldier and Michael Cooksey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Billy Pettit
assets.description: Billy Ray Pettit recalls a faceless stranger who told him how to free the driver in a crash near Baldwin, Wisconsin. He also remembers the principal at Greasy opening a package holding a check, a football and new clothes.
assets.about:
Before dawn on a road near Baldwin, Wisconsin, Billy Ray Pettit came upon a crash that had killed a young woman. A stranger with no face told him how to force the jammed door and hold the injured driver's head until help arrived; the state troopers found nobody else there. Eight months later the driver phoned to say his neck had been broken in three places: "You saved my life." Born in 1962, Billy started school at Greasy, where his brothers walked out of their own classrooms to sit beside him on his first day. Listen as he recalls principal Nellie Mayes marching him to her office and opening a package holding a $500 check, a football and new clothes, and on the seventy-two pounds of beans he cooked for festival tacos. Billy's is a record of providence, and of help arriving from places he cannot explain.

The interviewers are Dianna Guffey and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Senora Sixkiller-King
assets.description: Senora Sixkiller-King recounts castrating a hog as a girl to become a hog raiser, following her healer grandfather through the woods to learn medicinal plants, and helping her husband Don through the aftermath of Vietnam.
assets.about:
When her father was away, Senora Sixkiller-King castrated a hog herself before throwing the remains into a tree – if they stayed put, you would become a hog raiser. Born in 1957, one of nine, Senora grew up in flour-sack dresses and making do with little, but it was a life that was rich in other resources. She followed her grandfather Degatlagi, a healer, through the woods, learning the plants that could heal. Listen as she recalls her mother running from a headless figure, helping her husband Don deal with the ravages of the Vietnam War, and the children they raised when they could have none of their own. Her story offers a vivid, plainspoken view into traditional Cherokee life.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Michael Cooksey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.description: Sneaking into the garden for cherry tomatoes with salt and getting chased with a switch at Granny's creek, Keith Gonzales shares a childhood that led to twenty-five years catching chickens as an adult.
assets.about:
The year Keith Gonzales was born, his father built their log house, writing his son’s birth date into the cement. Listen as he recalls sneaking into the garden to eat cherry tomatoes with salt, climbing bendy trees with his older brother Doxie, and being chased with a switch at Granny's creek. As an adult he caught chickens for twenty-five years, eight or ten at a time, working day and night. This is a picture of childhood in one of the small, isolated Cherokee settlements made up almost entirely of a single family.

The interviewers are Guy Soldier and Dianna Guffey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.title: Jerry Bigfeather
assets.description: Jerry Bigfeather reflects on growing up in Bunch, Oklahoma, one of ten children raised by Walter and Enda Bigfeather in a two-story home, cooking on a propane stove. He recalls a childhood of hunting, swimming, and subsistence farming, tending cows and donkeys named Jake and Kate, alongside a garden his mother canned.
assets.about:
Jerry Bigfeather reflects on growing up in Bunch, Oklahoma, one of ten children raised by Walter and Enda Bigfeather in a two-story home, cooking on a propane stove. He recalls a childhood of hunting, swimming, and subsistence farming, tending cows and donkeys named Jake and Kate, alongside a garden his mother canned. After Cave Springs and Northeastern State University, Jerry built a long career with Cherokee Nation, moving from construction to housing inspector in 1990 and now working in environmental health. He remembers his father hauling hay and cutting wood, and working nights at Stilwell Foods alongside family. Married 45 years with two children and three grandchildren, Jerry is also an accomplished fiddle player who composes his own music. He reflects candidly on his belief that the Cherokee language will eventually be lost.

assets.about:
Sisters Lucy Anderson and Emma Jean Falling grew up in Locust Grove. The dogs would begin circling in excitement whenever Grandma put on her cap, handing each girl a lard bucket and a homemade gig for catching crawdads at Spring Creek. Feather mattresses were dragged outside so everyone could sleep under the stars and wake up wet with dew. Hear them on the $300 of wild onions their mother once sold in Tulsa, on organ music played at midnight in a stern great-grandmother's house. Emma tells of her forty years at Hillcrest and the flower arranging she took up to keep her spirits up when her son fell ill. A record of Cherokee grandmothers and aunts raising children, and what the sisters carry of it afterwards.

Eugene and Betty Nofire have been married for nearly fifty years. Listen in as the couple talk about growing up in Oak Ridge and Fog Hollow, in rural homes with no electricity. The couple look back on being raised as exclusive Cherokee speakers, and the steep language barriers they faced at school as a result.

As adults, Eugene and Betty both worked long hours in local factories and raised children on their rural property. Their account includes lighthearted stories about country life – like a scalded hog that led them on a wild chase around the farm. Warm and full of humor, their story is one of hardship, community, and lifelong devotion.

assets.about:
Russell Beaver grew up on five acres of his grandfather's land at Caney, where the creek ran past the house and never once dried up, and where he swam and hunted crawdads with his friends. Hear him on night hunting with good dogs, on the watercress at the spring they called fire in the water, and on peaches, green beans, and even fish put up in jars for Christmas. The five acres are still in the family, and he is working on getting a trailer out there so he can move home. Russell's memories show how completely a family can belong to one small piece of ground, and how strong the pull back to it remains.

Ross Gonzales grew up swimming in creeks and sleeping under the stars on Ross Mountain, near Rock Fence. Here, he recalls his early life – from sitting and listening to elders who spoke "long Cherokee", to an incredible story about seeing mythical Little People crossing a flooded creek.

Ross reflects on twenty-three years with the Cherokee Nation and a lifetime of dangerous jobs. He emphasizes ancestral warnings against family infighting and the need to guide younger generations with wisdom from elders. His story captures a boyhood rich in Cherokee tradition and spiritual wonder.

assets.about:
Jerry Cochran and Henry Sawney grew up as neighbors in an all-Cherokee community near Salem. In this interview, they reminisce about a childhood of inventive games, like racing weed flowers and rolling dirt-filled tires down the road. They talk about living the Cherokee cultural concept of Gadugi – or working together – on community woodcutting days.

Jerry served in Vietnam, then worked as a police officer, while Henry worked on farms, picking potatoes and cutting broom corn. Together, they swap humorous local lore and Gadugi in practice: the unpaid, unglamorous work that held a community together.

assets.about:
Roy Grimmett was born in Bunch in 1944, and raised near Greasy. At eighty-two, he looks back on being orphaned at age eleven, enduring corporal punishment at school for speaking Cherokee, and picking cotton in mile-long rows. Roy holds extensive knowledge of traditional herbal remedies, including the use of sagebrush for fevers and yellow wood tea for kidney stones. He's also an expert slingshot marksman. Roy's story reflects resilience in the face of loss and hardship.

The interviewer is Dianna Guffey, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

Neighbors would swing kerosene lanterns down the mountain to visit – conversations the young Watie was allowed to listen in on. He recalls his father and a neighbor calling each other out to the all-night fox hunt on cow horns, and potatoes stored under the house to last the winter. Doris Shell was born at home in Bunch and learned to cook on a wood stove at age nine while standing on a milk crate. Her memories offer an affectionate look at traditional Cherokee education and culture.

Now, she preserves traditional medicines passed down by her mother, and fiercely advocated for teaching Cherokee to her grandchildren. Katie's experience goes to the heart of Cherokee identity, and of who gets to certify it.

Born in 1962 as one of seven children, Cora Flute drew cold well water morning and evening, with everyone drinking from the one dipper. Listen as she remembers details from her childhood: using leaves as play money, serving pretend meals off clay plates, building toy boats powered by rubber bands, and riding bicycles everywhere in the summer heat. When her mother died, young people in the community cooked and cleaned for the family, and kept a ritual fire going for three or four nights. Cora’s story is one of loss, community support, and childhood joy despite hardship.

assets.description: Following his father everywhere as a boy, Jerry Ice remembers riding workhorses and a bluish ball of light over Molly Fields Cemetery. He also talks about Vietnam, the PTSD that followed, and the support he found from Cherokee Nation elders.
assets.about:
Jerry Ice and his father were always close. Born in Borger, Texas, Jerry’s family moved to Oklahoma when he was six years old. Listen as he talks about following his father everywhere, riding workhorses, and storing turnips in a straw-lined hole for winter. He remembers marvelling at the bluish ball of light over Molly Fields Cemetery, which his father called fox fire. Jerry cut broom in Colorado as a young man, and got laughed at for cutting stalks all over the field instead of in a row. Later, he joined the army and ended up in Vietnam. He talks about the PTSD that followed, and the support he received from Cherokee Nation elders. Now an elder himself, Jerry looks back on a life of loss and trauma – and the family and community that helped him make it through.

assets.about:
The little people have a road through Dorothy Ice's yard, and when the Cherokee Nation set her new house down, the spare bedroom landed right on it. Now she hears them rattling her metal lids at night, and leaves cookies out for them. Born at midnight on 26 December 1935 in a one-room house her father built in the woods, she wore dresses her mother sewed from four flour sacks. Follow along with her memories of a cart built from stroller wheels and her father's big nails, a car fender dragged up an icy ridge for a sled, hunting squirrels so her mother could make dumplings. This is a portrait of a Cherokee woman who took on the work usually left to men, and never once slowed down.

assets.about:
Four years ago, specialists told Richard Lee Ross he had months to live – a miracle he attributes to a higher power. He still lives in the house he grew up in on Ross Mountain, where about fifteen Ross households once shared one road in and out. Outsiders joked they might get thrown to the family's pigs. Listen as he recalls Saturday mornings at the junk pile building bicycles, pulling a drowning girl out of a flooding creek by her hair, training horses, and turning down a book deal. Richard speaks with the authority of a man raised inside Cherokee healing traditions, including what they forbid.

assets.description: Growing up at Briggs and Rocky Ford, James and Patsy Reese remember drawing spring water, playing jacks and kick the can, and how James first noticed Patsy at an All-Indian baseball tournament, watching her instead of the game.
assets.about:
When water was finally piped to the house, James Reese threw the bucket out of the house in celebration. When television arrived, he watched it all night long. He and wife Patsy grew up at Briggs and Rocky Ford, drawing water from a spring, swimming and catching crawdads, playing jacks and kick the can — and he first noticed her at an All-Indian baseball tournament at Northeastern, watching her instead of the game. Hear them on salting pork and keeping potatoes in hay in a dark cellar, on neighbors cutting wood and butchering together, and on James playing first base at Sequoyah for the team that took second at state in 1965. A shared life built on very little, and the rural institutions that carried two families through it.

assets.description: Raised near Peavine, Sallie Luethje remembers a leaking two-room log cabin, crawdads from the creek, and learning to drive by the age of eight. She also speaks plainly about her grandmother's land being fenced away bit by bit, and her twenty-five years at the Jack Brown Center.
assets.about:
Older girls pulled Sallie into a fifth-grade softball game, she hit the ball out of sight. Born on the last day of 1947 and raised near Peavine, she lost her father to TB at five, and remembers the whole community keeping vigil, everyone holding his hand. Follow along with her memories of a two-room log cabin that leaked, onions hanging from the eaves, crawdads cooked down by Peavine Creek, picking strawberries at seven for fifty cents an hour, and learning to drive by the time she was eight. She spent twenty-five years at the Jack Brown Center with young people fighting addiction. Sallie maps the harms visited on a Cherokee community across a lifetime. She speaks plainly about her grandmother's land fenced away bit by bit, and about the meth that took young men, her own son among them.

The interviewers are Linda Hammer and Dianna Guffey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.about:
At 80, their grandfather was still diving into the river and walking to the store for Pepsi until a passing truck knocked him down. Cousins GW Beaver and Donald Adair grew up in Greasy with the same grandparents, swinging from grapevines – and smoking them, until their grandfather walked past laughing at his dizzy grandsons. Listen in as they swap stories of coon hunting at midnight with Uncle Jack and a kerosene lamp, Sesliy Feathers, a dog named Understand, and on the preacher who fled from an owl’s hoot. Tracing their lineage along the Trail of Tears, the cousins balance their lighthearted tales with poignant historical consciousness of identity and cultural endurance. These cousins show storytelling and humor is a way a Cherokee family can keep its past alive.

The interviewer is Guy Soldier, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.about:
Kenneth and Norma Littledeer grew up in Bell, Oklahoma, and raised their family in the same tiny settlement. Listen as they talk about tough but happy childhoods, and years spent in the Cherokee community. Kenneth remembers spending his own money on a Bible for his mother– the encouragement she needed to learn to read. Norma lived in a small house with fourteen people, where the washing was done in the creek and meals were gravy, beans and bread. The couple talks about their decades together – the Bell boxing club that kept their boys going in their younger days, and using mustard tied in brown paper to ease a feverish child. Their story explores love, faith and marriage through hardship.

Cousins Weynama Smith and Wanda Robertson talk about their Webber ancestors, who fled Arkansas before removal and settled at what is now Webber’s Falls – they opened a store to provide cheap food to Cherokee families coming from the Trail of Tears. assets.about:
Sam Daugherty didn’t have a comfortable childhood. After losing his parents as a small boy, he was passed between relatives, then eventually raised by a white couple in Texas. Listen as he talks about a childhood in the Cherokee community before the adoption – his grandfather Scott Big Deer killing sixteen hogs, and far flung neighbors coming in to help butcher them; his grandmother gathering spiderwort in the woods; and milk from the farm left in the spring for anyone who needed it. Sam details how he once threw a guard into the water during a dramatic escape from an island work camp in California. The pair talk about their life, Diane learning to drive the trucks so Sam could sleep as they drove, and the challenges that come with being visibly Cherokee on the road.

assets.about:
Mike and Roger Glass share a wide-ranging, richly detailed account of growing up in Greasy without electricity until Mike was nine, raising owls and other wild animals as pets, and hunting and fishing constantly as boys. Mike recounts a gripping, extended story of nearly being chased by a massive rattlesnake through the woods before finally killing it, and both brothers recall their grandmother's traditional healing, pressing burning-hot coals against pain with her bare hands. They reflect candidly on regional Cherokee dialect differences, discussing how pronunciation shifts from community to community, and share their shared fear that the old, precise vocabulary for everyday things is fading as fewer people use it daily. Mike traces a long working life, including 42 years at a local company, while Roger recalls singing in Cherokee at gatherings across the region. The interview offers an exceptionally rich, often hilarious account of tradition, humor and language preservation in Greasy.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.about: Bob Pettit shares an extraordinarily detailed account of subsistence life near South Bunch and Hickory Van Hollow, recalling childhood chores like hauling creek water during a 1960 drought and helping his mother pound clothes clean on a grooved washing rock. Interviewed by Charlie, he vividly recounts the excitement of a soldier returning home by train, and years spent making shingles, fence posts, and railroad ties alongside his father. Bob describes in rich detail traditional food preservation — drying fish and fruit on rooftops, storing potatoes beneath prairie grass through winter, and making lye soap and hominy from scratch — alongside Cherokee names for tools and plants he's careful to teach the listeners. He reflects candidly on losing several siblings young to an unexplained illness elders attributed to "nerve sickness," and closes with a sober warning that fluent Cherokee conversation, not just classroom teaching, is nearly gone. The interview offers an exceptionally rich account of Cherokee self-sufficiency, food traditions and hard-won wisdom.

assets.about:
Levi Eagle and John Lee Soap share memories of growing up together in Sequoyah County, both born at Hastings Hospital into a family shaped by farming, faith and tradition. John recalls his father's knowledge as a medicine man, a body of traditional healing he once learned but has since largely forgotten, along with lessons from his mother. Levi, meanwhile, remembers his own childhood playing baseball and softball as a catcher, and the family's regular walks to church after his mother dedicated a place of worship to the community during her lifetime. He also explains the origin of his nickname, Jug, earned from making cider. Together, their recollections offer a warm, complementary window into one Cherokee family's history of land, medicine, faith and community in Sequoyah County.

assets.about: Billy Teehee recalls a childhood spent in the Fog Hollow community near Salem, Oklahoma, where he was raised by his grandparents, Tsali and Wonidi, alongside eight siblings after being given up as an infant. Speaking only Cherokee until he started school, he shares memories of subsistence life on land given to the family by tribal members: hand-hewn railroad ties cut with an axe, a three-acre garden, hog butchering, and a neighbor woman who served as the community's healer using medicine from the woods. He describes hunting squirrels with dogs and rocks, playing homemade-bat baseball against nearby Cherokee communities, and later spending decades as a chicken catcher before settling into long careers at a Siloam Springs electric plant and Lowe's. Now often the only Cherokee speaker where he lives, he still seeks out old friends to converse in the language. The interview offers a vivid, firsthand picture of everyday Cherokee family and community life across much of the twentieth century.

assets.about: Charley Dewy Keener shares memories of growing up along Fourteen Mile Creek near Lost City, in a close Cherokee-speaking community made up almost entirely of his own extended family. He recalls the hardship of being sent to boarding school at Wyandotte, where he was punished for speaking Cherokee and struggled to understand English, and describes returning home after his grandmother's death to finish school at Hulbert. The interview traces his path from farm chores and traditional foods like kunichi to a working life as an ironworker, building radio and telephone towers hundreds of feet tall across the country. He reflects candidly on childhood fears of white neighbors, his mother's stories of the little people who lived on the hill, and his worry that the Cherokee language is fading even as his grandchildren pursue careers in medicine and nursing. The recording offers a personal account of one man's journey between two worlds, and his hope that Cherokee endures.

assets.about:
Eddie Bird reflects on a childhood in Greasy, originally called Zion, one of seven siblings in a large extended family. He traces a 28-year career as a long-haul truck driver, hauling dog food and auto parts across 48 states on a demanding weekly schedule. Much of the conversation turns to family history, including the surname "Bird" possibly descending from "Longbird," and a striking mid-interview discovery that he and the interviewer may be distant cousins. Eddie shares inherited stories of wartime protective medicine meant to make bullets miss their target, and fondly recalls childhood adventures swimming near the dam, riding bikes on dirt roads, and a funny mix-up that earned him the nickname "Scorpion" after insisting a scorpion was "almost a crawdad." The interview offers a warm, often funny account of family, work and community in the Greasy area.

She recalls her mother teaching her to cook and her grandfather's traditional remedies, from removing warts with matches to sumac berries steeped for her father's blood pressure. She shares lively childhood memories of sibling fights, a hunting accident that sent a friend into a panic, and family cooking traditions like water gravy and fried bread. Bernice reflects candidly and with quiet resignation that she believes the Cherokee language will eventually come to an end, even as she takes comfort in her faith. assets.description: Ernest Johnson recalls growing up in Bunch and Greasy with twin older brothers, farm work raising pigs and chickens, and years spent building bridges in Barling before quitting school and taking up auto body repair.

Ernest Johnson reflects on growing up in the Bunch and Greasy area, one of several siblings including twin older brothers, Ronald and Donald. He recalls farm labor raising pigs and chickens, and a family life largely free of conflict, quitting school at Cave Springs in ninth grade after an injury from football. Ernest traces work building bridges in Barling, recalling a colleague's fall from the structure, and shares that he taught himself auto body repair and painting, a skill he still practices today. He reflects on childhood school discipline, including memories of being paddled, and a sibling's stint at boarding school with only occasional passes home. The interview offers a grounded, if partial, account of family, farm labor and craftsmanship in the Bunch and Greasy communities.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.title: Clifford Bark
assets.description: After four years squinting from the back of the classroom, Clifford Bark was finally driven to Muskogee for glasses. He also shares memories of rebuilding his father's truck engine at fourteen, an enormous dog named Moon, and stingy Little People at Spavinaw.
assets.about:
As a child, Clifford Bark spent four years at the back of the classroom, unable to make out what the teacher was writing. She moved him to a closer desk, and less than a month later, he and five classmates were driven to Muskogee for glasses. Listen as Clifford recalls coming out of the appointment with his eyes dilated, and going home with his eyes shut. At fourteen, Clifford rebuilt his father's truck engine – much to his father’s amazement. He talks about the family dog, Moon, an enormous creature that arrived in settlement of a debt, and a night at Spavinaw when the Little People proved stingy with the crawdads. His story reflects a childhood of hardship, wonder, and Cherokee tradition.

The interviewer is Guy Soldier, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.title: Johnny Lee Jumper Sr
assets.description: One of eight children, Johnny Lee Jumper remembers pushing dirt-filled flat irons to make "smoke," the one house with a TV, midnight singing gatherings at Bull Holler, and Little People rattling around the kitchen.
assets.about:
Johnny Lee Jumper grew up around Kenwood, Oklahoma. Listen as he talks about growing up as one of eight, pushing old flat irons filled with dirt to make "smoke" at his grandma's, and gathering at the one house with a TV to watch until ten at night. Johnny’s family moved between country settlements and industrial towns, following the work. Still, he recalls singing gatherings at Bull Holler that ran until midnight, his Uncle Redbird, who would drink only spring water because "it was medicine," and the Little People who came into the house and rattled around the kitchen. His story is about traditions mixing with modern life, and culture enduring despite it all.

The interviewer is Guy Soldier, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.about: Kathy Van Buskirk grew up as one of eight children in a Cherokee family in northeastern Oklahoma, in a home shaped by family, faith and Cherokee culture. A full-blood Cherokee woman, Kathy has spent much of her life helping carry Cherokee knowledge forward. She is an accomplished traditional basket maker and was named a Cherokee National Treasure in 2004, while her husband Perry was recognised for traditional bow making. Kathy has also worked in Cherokee language revitalisation, including with the Cherokee Immersion School, helping support a new generation of speakers. Through her art, language work and storytelling, she has remained deeply committed to family and to passing Cherokee culture and knowledge on to future generations.

assets.description: Dewitt and Anna Teehee have watched Jay change slowly over the decades. He recalls the one-teacher country school at Uregan and being made squad leader at Fort Bliss simply for being "big enough."
assets.about:
Anna Teehee was born at home near Piney Church, which lets her husband Dewitt tease that she was born in the woods. They have watched Jay change slowly over the decades: a chicken factory that opened and has since closed, a Dollar General, a clinic. Listen as he recalls the country school at Uregan, twenty-eight children and one teacher, where the big kids helped teach the little ones, on being made a squad leader at Fort Bliss simply because he was "big enough," which spared him kitchen duty. Observing Jay's slow development over decades, the Teehees note that while factories and stores have changed, the fundamental warmth and solidarity of the Cherokee community remain the same.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language speaker (with Mitch Holcomb present).

assets.title: Louise Hubbard & Anna Louise Vann
assets.description: Louise Hubbard and Anna Louise Vann met as young women picking cotton out west, dragging hundred-pound sacks. They share memories of the Sevenstar Brothers quartet and the yellow wood tea Louise still drinks every morning.
assets.about:
Louise Hubbard and Anna Louise Vann met as young women, picking cotton out west. While the work was back-breaking – dragging hundred-pound gunny sacks and being paid by weight, the women both claim they had fun growing up. Listen as the two talk about their early lives in the Cherokee community. Anna’s father sang in the Sevenstar Brothers quartet, going around Cherokee churches all over the country. Louise talks about her grandfather, who lived to over 100, teaching her to make Yellow Wood tea. She still drinks it every single morning. She talks about the rituals involved with Cherokee medicine – praying before you gather a plant or root – and how one root medicine brought her husband’s blood sugar down.

The interviewers are Guy Soldier and Mitch Holcomb, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.description: Six fluent speakers share humor, stories and insights into what it means to think and speak in Cherokee, and why the language must be lived rather than simply learned.
assets.about: This roundtable brings together six fluent Cherokee speakers for a lively discussion about what it truly means to think and speak as a Cherokee. The group explores how humor functions as "medicine" for hard times, and how spoken Cherokee paints vivid mental pictures in ways English cannot fully capture. They trade humorous personal stories, including a memorable exchange between a hungry Cherokee boy and a confused white settler, and debate the accuracy of Bible translations and classroom Cherokee against the language they grew up speaking at home. Much of the conversation turns to dialect differences across regions, from Bell to North Carolina, and shared concern that words for traditional knowledge, medicine, and the natural world are fading simply from disuse. The group closes with a call for learners to live and think in Cherokee rather than memorize it from books, insisting fluency must come from the heart. The interview offers a rare, candid glimpse into how fluent Cherokee speakers relate to their language, humor and each other.

assets.description: Marion "Jr." Scraper recalls a childhood without running water in a small home, hauling fences and rails, learning English at seven, and later swimming, fishing and playing basketball at Haskell before Cherokee Nation sent him for ironwork training.
assets.about:
Marion "Jr." Scraper reflects on a childhood shaped by hard work and family. Raised by his mother with no full siblings, he recalls a small childhood home and the labor of making fence posts and rails growing up. He didn't speak English when he started school at seven, but learned quickly, later attending Haskell, where he met his wife and played basketball after one rough day of football. Marion remembers growing up without running water, hauling it from a spring, and his mother's fluency in both Cherokee and a little Creek. He shares lighter memories too, including tricks played by half-siblings and an accidental deer hunt out of season, alongside summers spent swimming and fishing on the Sallisaw River. After graduating, he worked briefly at Stilwell Canning Factory before Cherokee Nation sent him to Indiana and Tulsa for ironwork training.

The interviewer is Michael Cooksey, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.about:
Pernell Vann was born in Tahlequah in 1970 and raised in Greasy, one of three childre. He recalls a childhood of fishing, riding bikes, and visiting elders, attending grade school in Greasy before Cave Springs, where he played football. The family had electricity but no running water, and Pernell remembers getting their first television as a young child, watching cartoons and I Love Lucy. After graduating, he worked in New Mexico before eventually settling into work in Arkansas. He shares memories of a close-knit community where people would walk long distances to visit, and reflects on his own family today, including two daughters and a grandson. Pernell also recalls learning about traditional Indian medicine, and looking back with concern on how much children have changed since his own upbringing.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Dianna Guffey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

Senora Sixkiller-King shares memories of growing up in Little Kansas in a Cherokee-speaking family, where life centred on family, food, the land, and knowledge passed down through generations. She recalls gathering wild foods, canning, sewing, raising animals, preparing traditional foods, and helping with large family and church meals.

A strong thread through her story is the knowledge she learned from her grandfather, a healer. By following him through the woods, she learned about plants, medicines, and traditional ways of caring for people. Senora also reflects on starting school without speaking English, having fewer people to speak Cherokee with today, and the importance of sharing this knowledge so it continues for future generations.

His family kept a hillside garden, raised pigs and chickens, plowed with donkeys, and stored food in a smokehouse he still maintains today, now home to his daughter. After Cave Springs and playing basketball and baseball, John joined the Army and completed two tours, spending time in Panama, Fort Benning, and Alaska. He remembers gathering traditional remedies like sassafras, and foraging wild and possum grapes.

assets.description: Marie Bird recalls moving from Oaks to Chewey at three, her mother's work at a canning factory, and growing up in a crowded one-room house, before raising eight children and working at a nursing home until retirement.
assets.about:
Marie Bird was born at home in Oaks and moved to Chewey at age three, one of three Cherokee-speaking siblings in a farming family. She recalls her mother taking in laundry and working at a canning factory, picking strawberries and beans as a child, and a big garden tended with horses. After her brother turned twelve, her father left the family. Marie attended school at Sequoyah and graduated from Bacone, later working at a nursing home before retiring. She raised eight children - none of them fluent speakers, though they understand the language - and has twenty grandchildren. She recalls the family's first car being a Model T with no heater, and the crowded one-room house she grew up in.

The interviewers are Charlie Shell and Dianna Guffey, respected Cherokee first language speakers.

assets.description: Nancy Kingfisher recalls growing up in Little Kansas and Salina, picking strawberries and beans as her father made fence posts, before twenty years in Tulsa and a long career at a casino.
assets.about:
Nancy Kingfisher grew up in Little Kansas and Salina before finishing school and later moving to Tulsa, where she lived for twenty years. One of six siblings, she recalls her father making fence posts and tending a garden to support the family, and picking strawberries and green beans as a child while her mother worked the garden and cared for the children. She remembers her family's knowledge of earache remedies and her mother's fluency reading Cherokee. Only she and her brother remain fluent speakers today. In Tulsa, she worked briefly at an internet business before spending twelve years at a casino.

The interviewer is Michael Cooksey, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.about:
Sandra Soap and Loretta Barrios, sisters from a family of four, recall growing up speaking Cherokee in Nicut, and attending school there through eighth grade - though their youngest sibling no longer speaks the language. Loretta didn't attend high school and later worked various jobs in Fort Smith; Sandra attended briefly and went on to work caring for the elderly. Both married men with some understanding of Cherokee, and their own children retain partial fluency. They recall relying on medicine from the woods rather than doctors, though the specifics have faded with time. The sisters also share lighter memories, including Sandra's belief in Bigfoot and a story of seeing a red sphere near Wilson Rock as a child.

The interviewer is Charlie Shell, respected Cherokee first language speaker.

assets.title: Nancy Crispiano
assets.description: Nancy Crispiano recalls growing up in Bunch, Oklahoma, as one of eight Cherokee-speaking siblings, with fond memories of a peach tree that produced plenty of fruit.
assets.about:
Nancy Crispiano reflects on growing up in Bunch, Oklahoma, one of eight Cherokee-speaking siblings in a home with far less crowding and development than today. She recalls the difficulty of starting school without English, gradually learning with help from classmates, and remembers a productive peach tree alongside a wood stove and well that sustained the family. After attending Cave Springs, she left school in the twelfth grade to help at home, relying on self-sufficiency rather than doctor visits. Nancy later worked at a chicken processing plant in Bentonville before returning to care for her parents, and most recently worked in the cafeteria at Stilwell Hospital. She now lives with her daughter and two grandsons.

The interviewer is Michael Cooksey, respected Cherokee first language speaker.
